title: Major study into 'forever chemicals' in people's bodies launched in UK
summary: The government is launching the first study to measure PFAS in the UK population to understand the risks.
text: PFAS: Major study into 'forever chemicals' in UK population - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Science Major study into 'forever chemicals' in people's bodies launched in UK Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Forever chemicals - or PFAS - can enter the human body after leaking into soil and waterways By Laura Foster Inside Health presenter, BBC Radio 4 Published 3 November 2026 The government is launching its first study into the levels of so-called 'forever chemicals' in the UK population. By taking blood and urine samples, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) hopes to gain a better understanding of any potential health risks caused by the substances also known as PFAS, as well as other potential contaminants like lead and arsenic. It said current evidence suggested the possible health impacts associated with PFAS are likely to be limited, but said the strongest links found in large population groups have been to raised cholesterol and lower birth weights. The first results are expected next year. PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) have been used prolifically since the 1940s and 1950s because they are resistant to water, oil and heat. It is why they have been placed in thousands of items such as pots and pans, clothing and foams used to fight fires. But because they do not break down easily in the environment - hence the name 'forever chemicals' - they have raised health concerns in recent years. Two are already banned in the UK - PFOA and PFOS - because prolonged exposure to them can increase the risk of cancer, according to the World Health Organization. , external But the study of PFAS is an emerging field with more than 15,000 types to research. The UKHSA will take blood and urine samples collected through the existing Health Survey for England , external to establish baseline levels of PFAS, lead, arsenic, bisphenols, phthalates and flame retardants in the population. Inside Health: What we do and don't know about PFAS Listen on R4 at 09:30 or on BBC Sounds Listen on Sounds In an exclusive interview with BBC Radio 4's Inside Health, Dr Edward Wynne-Evans, director of radiation, chemicals, climate and environmental hazards at the UKHSA, said there are gaps around "what different levels of exposure mean for an individual's long-term health". There are growing concerns among people living near sites where there has been contamination from the two known toxic PFAS, and they have chosen to get individual blood tests. In September, blood tests found "really high levels" of one of the cancer-causing forever chemicals (PFOA) in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory. But the UK government does not recommend individuals get routine PFAS blood testing because there is no "established clinical intervention" if they have elevated levels, Wynne-Evans said. "If you are going to do a test where you cannot recommend an action to follow, we would not normally recommend a test." He said that this study would help "build an evidence base to better understand what might be happening". Speaking before this study was announced, Prof Tony Fletcher from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine said he believed there is a low level of PFAS in everyone's blood. "If we tested a random sample of anybody's blood, we would measure [PFAS] in low levels." "We are not all dying because of this but at higher levels [and in larger populations] they have been associated with adverse health effects." For the two banned PFAS - PFOA and PFOS - the known risks , external include increased cholesterol, an increased risk of cancer, reduced antibody levels following childhood vaccinations and a range of endocrine effects linked to the thyroid and lower birth weights. "I have met with people living in an area with contamination - they are angry," Fletcher said. "What I try and explain to them is we have found these causal associations between exposure and effect in studying large populations. Although at an individual level, the chances of you getting some bad disease or some adverse health effect is quite low." He stated the important thing is to stop ongoing exposure, to avoid any long-term effects.
